message.content:
A **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** and a **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating system tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally built to render graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Core Count** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for single‑thread performance. | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores optimized for executing many threads simultaneously. |
| **Clock Speed** | Higher clock speeds (often >3 GHz) because each core does complex work. | Lower clock speeds (1–2 GHz) because each core is simpler; performance comes from sheer number of cores. |
| **Architecture** | Complex control logic, deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler, highly parallel architecture with many arithmetic units, less sophisticated control logic. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies on fast shared memory and texture caches; often uses GDDR memory with very high bandwidth. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching code, I/O handling, OS kernel operations. | Data‑parallel workloads: matrix/vector math, image/video processing, rendering, neural network inference/training. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or few‑threaded code, often written in C/C++/Java, executed on the host CPU. | Parallel kernels written in CUDA/OpenCL/DirectX/Vulkan, executed on the device GPU. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power consumption per core when idle, but can consume more power under heavy load due to higher clock speeds. | Very efficient at performing many simple operations per watt, especially for data‑parallel tasks. |

### Why the Difference Matters

- **Performance**: For tasks that can be split into many independent sub‑tasks (e.g., matrix multiplication), a GPU can outperform a CPU by orders of magnitude because it processes all sub‑tasks concurrently.
- **Flexibility**: CPUs handle a wide variety of tasks, including those with irregular control flow, whereas GPUs excel when the same operation is applied repeatedly across large data sets.
- **Cost & Power**: GPUs provide higher throughput for specific workloads but may be overkill for general-purpose tasks. CPUs are cheaper and more versatile for everyday use.

In short, a CPU is like a master chef who can cook many dishes one at a time quickly and adaptively, while a GPU is like a factory line that can produce thousands of identical items simultaneously.
